paper.title: Does schooling increase or reduce inequality in achievement and conscientiousness in Denmark?
paper.journal: Research in Social Stratification and Mobility
paper.code_data_availability: Data Availability (p. 11): 'The data used for this study is not publicly available and cannot be shared as it is based on individual-level administrative records. …

variables_mentioned: parents' highest level of education (observed the year the child was born)
ISCO codes used to construct ISEI (HISEI)

registers.role: outcome (self-reported conscientiousness) and classroom-disorder control; sample frame for the survey dataset
variables_mentioned: 'How often can you complete what you set out to do?'
'If interrupted during lessons, I can quickly concentrate again?'

classroom disorder items ('If there is noise in the classroom, the teachers can quickly restore order?', 'Is it easy to hear what the teacher says during lessons?', 'Is it easy to hear what the other students say during lessons?')

registers.name_in_paper: National reading comprehension test (Danish national tests, Ministry of Education)
registers.role: outcome (reading achievement); sample frame for the test dataset

registers.name_in_paper: National math test (used as a sensitivity check)

linkages: Danish Student Well-being Survey results and national reading comprehension test results linked at the individual level to Danish administrative register data
Children linked to their parents for parental education, ISEI/HISEI and parental age
Siblings identified in the register data for the sibling fixed effects robustness models
Children linked to schools (school fixed effects) and to classrooms (classroom disorder, constructed as a classroom average excluding the focal student)

sample.universe: Children in Danish public schools taking the mandatory Danish Student Well-being Survey (grades 0–8, 2015–2019) or the mandatory national reading comprehension test (grades 2, 4, 6 and 8, 2010–2019)
sample.unit_of_observation: child × grade (one observation per child per survey/test occasion); models are estimated separately by grade
selection_rules: Only students starting school in the year they turn six (the official school starting age)
Only students whose age fits the designated age of their class
Exclude children taking the survey or the test outside the officially stipulated period or on a different date than their classmates
Exclude children who attend special education
Exclude children who are younger or older than the designated age for their class
Survey responses used for 2015–2019; reading test responses used for 2010–2019

construction_notes: School exposure = date of survey/test minus date of school start in grade 0, precise to the day but scaled as months; age = date of survey/test minus date of birth, likewise scaled as months.

Reading achievement: each of the three test domains standardized within grade and year, the three standardized values averaged, and the average standardized within grade and year again, so coefficients read as standard deviations.

Conscientiousness: index of three Big Five items in the grade 4–9 questionnaire and two of those items in the grade 0–3 questionnaire; Cronbach's alpha 0.68 (2015), 0.69 (2016), 0.70 (2017), 0.70 (2018), 0.70 (2019). One item ('How often can you complete what you set out to do?') shows differential item functioning across grades.
Classroom disorder: classroom average of three Ministry of Education items, excluding the focal student's own response.

Parental education coded in four categories (lower secondary or lower; vocational upper secondary; academic upper secondary and lower tertiary; master's or higher), observed the year the child was born; HISEI (ISEI from parental ISCO codes, averaged over parents) used as an alternative, standardized to mean zero and SD one.
Models include school fixed effects and dummies for the year the child answered the survey/test, and are estimated separately by grade.
Robustness samples: dropping children born October–December and January–March; sibling fixed effects; restricting to children surveyed/tested after the winter holiday and before Easter.

claims.statement: In grade 0, one additional month of school exposure lowers self-reported conscientiousness by about 0.028 SD.

definition.value: The difference between the date the child took the survey or test and the date they started school in grade 0, precise to the specific date but scaled as months. Conceived institutionally: exposure to the school year including weekends, after-school hours and holidays.

timing.value: Measured on the day of the survey/test in the given grade; the coefficient is the effect of one additional month of accumulated school exposure at that date.

outcome.label: Self-reported conscientiousness (standardized)

register_source.value: Danish Student Well-being Survey (DSWS), the mandatory annual school survey compiled by the Ministry of Education, linked to Danish administrative register data (no register code named)

definition.value: Standardized index of three Big Five Inventory items identified by a validation survey for the grade 4–9 questionnaire: 'How often can you complete what you set out to do?', 'Can you concentrate during lessons?' and 'If interrupted during lessons, I can quickly concentrate again?'. In grades 0–3 only the first two items are available. Cronbach's alpha 0.68–0.70 across 2015–2019.

timing.value: Self-reported on the day the child answers the mandatory survey in the given grade (survey years 2015–2019).

units.value: standard deviations of the grade- and year-standardized self-reported conscientiousness index per additional month of school exposure

magnitude.interpretation: The paper describes the overall result as 'a negative association of approximately -0.02 SD for each additional month of schooling across all grades'.

estimand.target_population: Danish public-school children in grade 0 who comply with the enrollment standard
estimand.time_horizon: contemporaneous: the effect of one additional month of school exposure on the outcome measured on the survey/test date

population.description: Children in grade 0 (ages 6–7) in Danish public schools answering the mandatory Danish Student Well-being Survey
population.selection: Students who started school in the calendar year they turned six and whose age fits the designated age of their class; children taking the survey/test outside the officially stipulated period or on a different date than their classmates, and children in special education, are excluded. Approximately 90 % of children comply with the enrollment standard.

identification.source_of_variation: Differential Exposure Approach: within-school variation in the date on which the mandatory survey/reading test is administered inside the Ministry of Education's two- to three-month field period, combined with a fixed school starting date (second week of August of the year the child turns six) and variation in birth dates, which separates months of school exposure from months of age.

key_assumptions.assumption: The dates on which schools administer the survey and the reading test are conditionally random: within the same school (and given year and background characteristics), the amount of school exposure a child has accumulated when tested is unrelated to parental SES and other determinants of the outcome.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Regressions predicting the test and survey dates on parental SES and child characteristics, run on the full sample (Tables A1, A4), with school fixed effects (Tables A2, A5) and on a reduced sample dropping children born October–December and January–March (Tables A3, A6); with school fixed effects SES generally does not predict the dates, apart from a few weak associations (e.g. parents with a master's degree take the eighth-grade test about half a day earlier).

key_assumptions.assumption: The estimation sample is conditioned on compliance with the enrollment standard (school start in the year the child turns six, age matching the class) and on taking the survey/test inside the stipulated period together with classmates; the estimates are for this selected group.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Section 3.1.1 states the exclusion rules; the author reports that approximately 90 % of children comply with the enrollment standards and that the balance check (Appendix B) shows low-SES children are less likely to comply.

implies_edges.from: Compliance with the official school starting age and the class-designated age

key_assumptions.assumption: Schooling and ageing are collinear and the Differential Exposure Approach decomposes the overall learning rate into the two; the schooling estimate is therefore only as good as the age-at-test estimate, and a linear additive separation of the two is assumed.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The author states that any bias in the age-at-test estimate will also affect the schooling estimate, and addresses it with a reduced sample and sibling fixed effects.

key_assumptions.assumption: The self-reported survey items measure conscientiousness itself rather than something that moves with the point of the school year at which the child answers (classroom disorder, declining motivation, school fatigue).
key_assumptions.supported_by: Robustness analysis adjusting for a classroom-level measure of disorder (Table H1); the author nonetheless states he cannot exclude that the negative effects capture school fatigue.

threats_discussed: School principals and teachers can choose when, inside the Ministry of Education's field period, to administer the survey/test, which could make the timing non-random

The field period overlaps with the winter and Easter holidays, which may be disruptive to learning or to test performance
The conscientiousness measure is self-reported and may pick up classroom disorder, declining motivation or school fatigue rather than personality
One conscientiousness item shows differential item functioning across grades

prior_findings_compared.as_stated: The negative effect of schooling on students' self-reported conscientiousness is in stark contrast to the findings of Cornelissen and Dustmann (2019), who found that schooling improves teachers' and parents' reports of students' non-cognitive skills.
The results are somewhat consistent with Jensen and Reimer (2021), who found improvements in students' self-reported well-being during the coronavirus lockdown using the same survey.
